title: "Sound 18: Chorus and Flanger"
toc: true

When a choir or a string section plays a note, no two players are exactly in tune or exactly in time.
The tiny differences make the sound wide and shimmering instead of one thin line. A **chorus** effect
fakes that with a single sound: it adds copies of the sound, each delayed by a few milliseconds, and
an [LFO](sound-lfo.qmd) keeps changing those delays.

**How to use the page.** The source starts as **chords**. Use headphones if you can: the copies are
spread left and right. The strip under the controls draws each copy's delay time over the last four
seconds.

## The effect

<div class="sk" data-w="chorus" data-source="chords"></div>

## Why a moving delay changes the pitch

A delay on its own only makes a sound later. But when the delay is **getting longer**, the sound
coming out is slowed down a little, so it's a little flat. When the delay is **getting shorter**, the
sound is sped up, so it's a little sharp. It's the Doppler effect of a passing siren. So an LFO on
the delay time is a gentle [vibrato](sound-lfo.qmd) on the copy. Mixed with the original, the
slightly detuned copy beats against it, and that beating is the shimmer.

Press **Vibrato**: the mix is 100% wet, so you hear only the moving copy. Its pitch wobbles. Now press
**Chorus** and the same wobble mixed with the dry sound becomes a shimmer.

## The controls

- **Delay**: the average delay. About 15 to 30 ms for chorus. Below 10 ms the copy no longer sounds
  like a separate player; above 35 ms it starts to sound like a slap-back echo (try **Doubler**: a
  single slowly moving copy at 35 ms sounds like the part was recorded twice).
- **Depth**: how far the delay swings, and so how far the pitch wobbles.
- **Rate**: how fast. Slow (0.3 to 1 Hz) is lush; fast is seasick.
- **Voices**: more copies, each with its own swing, spread across the stereo field.
- **Feedback**: feeds the delayed copy back into the delay.

## The flanger

Press **Flanger**. The delay is now very short (1 to 5 ms), and the feedback is high. At delays this
short the copy doesn't sound like a second player. Instead it cancels some frequencies and reinforces
others in an evenly spaced pattern, a **comb filter**. As the delay changes, the teeth of the comb
sweep up and down: the jet-plane "whoosh". It was first done with two tape machines running together,
an engineer pressing a thumb on the flange of one reel to slow it. Try it on the drum loop and on the
noise source, where the moving comb is easiest to see on the spectrum.
